anatomy.title: Hyoid bone · Structure & relationships · draft
anatomy.body: The hyoid lies in the anterior neck above the thyroid cartilage, with a body and greater/lesser horns. It has no direct bony articulation with another bone.
bullets: FJ2772 and FJ3201 are grouped under one hyoid identity; their union and extent require review. They are not certified body-versus-horn segments or evidence of a particular fusion age. The hyoid is not part of the skull proper.

bullets: The shadow blocks a view of tissue behind the bone; it is not the outline of the entire hyoid.
These descriptions come from a study of healthy adults. Its findings do not establish visibility in every neck or acquisition.

pathology.title: Hyoid bone · Injury & disease · draft
pathology.body: Hyoid injury can follow direct neck trauma, including sport or road collisions. Painful or difficult swallowing may accompany it; a hyoid fracture does not by itself establish the mechanism of injury.
bullets: Breathing difficulty or a new voice change after neck trauma needs urgent emergency assessment. Associated laryngeal injury must be considered separately.
This is a neck bone, not part of the skull proper. The two source components remain one hyoid selection; their separation is not a fracture line or a validated body/horn partition.

anatomy.title: Right hip bone · Structure & relationships · draft
anatomy.body: Each adult hip bone unites ilium, ischium and pubis around the acetabulum for the femoral head. It joins the sacrum posteriorly and the opposite pubis at the anterior symphysis.
bullets: One hip-bone surface is not three independently dissectible bones or the entire bony pelvis. Fusion timing, sex-specific pelvic shape, birth-canal dimensions and acetabular labrum are not established by this selection.
Reference bone surface: named landmarks, attachment footprints, cortical thickness and marrow are not independently segmented or validated. A cut surface is not an acquired CT section.

function.title: Right hip bone · Role & limits · draft

ct.title: Right hip bone · CT: follow the hip bone through the pelvis · draft
ct.body: Use the acetabulum to connect the ilium, ischium and pubis conceptually. On cross-sectional CT and its reformats, follow this bone beyond the socket rather than treating one acetabular slice as the entire hip bone.
bullets: Orient to the iliac crest superiorly, pubic rami anteriorly and ischial tuberosity posteroinferiorly. The sacrum and opposite hip bone provide the wider pelvic context.
This is one whole-bone surface, not separate acetabular columns, walls or a fracture map. Atlas cutaways do not reveal CT density; an isolated bone cannot assess the complete pelvic ring.
Source limit: whole-bone surface; named landmarks are teaching references, not separately validated segmentations.

ultrasound.body: At the anterior hip, distinguish the anterior superior iliac spine near sartorius and tensor fasciae latae from the anterior inferior iliac spine at the direct rectus femoris tendon attachment.
bullets: These iliac landmarks belong to the hip bone. The greater trochanter belongs to the neighbouring femur.

pathology.title: Right hip bone · Injury & disease · draft
pathology.body: Pelvic-ring injury and an acetabular fracture describe different anatomical problems: one concerns the ring, the other the hip socket. They can coexist.
bullets: High-energy pelvic injury may cause serious bleeding and associated organ injury and requires emergency assessment.
One hip bone is not the complete pelvic ring. Neither ligament competence, bleeding, bone density nor a patient-specific acetabular fracture is modelled.
pathology.note: Draft teaching; independent anatomical and clinical review pending. Educational context, not a patient diagnosis or treatment plan.

clinical.title: Right hip bone · Clinical context · draft
clinical.body: Distinguish the socket in the hip bone from the femoral head and neck. Evaluate pelvic stability in the context of the whole ring and its ligamentous connections.
bullets: For acetabular injury, location within the socket and joint congruity matter; a smooth atlas surface cannot show patient cartilage damage or displacement.
One hip bone is not the complete pelvic ring. Neither ligament competence, bleeding, bone density nor a patient-specific acetabular fracture is modelled.

ultrasound.title: Tenth thoracic vertebra · ultrasound orientation · draft
ultrasound.body: On a posterior thoracic sonogram, first separate the midline spinous-process echo from the adjacent laminar echoes. The bright accessible cortex casts a deeper acoustic shadow; the shadow is not a view through the vertebral body.
bullets: Moving laterally in the anatomy changes the expected bony landmark from lamina and articular column to transverse process, costotransverse region and rib. A rib echo and its shadow should not be renamed as the selected vertebra.

Ribs and overlapping posterior elements leave restricted interlaminar acoustic gaps. In an adult volunteer study, upper thoracic views were more often inconclusive than lower thoracic views; even a visible gap does not make the whole canal visible.

ultrasound.title: Second lumbar vertebra · ultrasound orientation · draft
ultrasound.body: On a posterior lumbar sonogram, a midline spinous-process echo and shadow orient the view. Just off midline, repeated laminar echoes alternate with interlaminar gaps; the gap is an acoustic window between bones, not a hole in the vertebra.
bullets: Farther lateral, the articular-process column and then the transverse-process echoes form different repeating patterns. Keep a facet-region echo distinct from the lamina and from the selected whole-vertebra mesh.

A phantom and small volunteer study delineated lumbar laminae, articular processes, transverse processes and L3/L4–L4/L5 interlaminar windows. Visibility through a window depends on the actual acquisition; it cannot be assumed from this model.

Toward the lower lumbar junction, the broad posterior sacral echo and the L5/S1 gap help orient relative position. Transitional anatomy can alter a level count, so neither this mesh label nor an isolated surface landmark verifies a patient’s L2–L5 numbering.

The superficial bone echo shadows what lies directly behind it. This atlas surface cannot inspect vertebral-body marrow, a disc or spinal cord, and no patient scan or atlas-to-patient registration is supplied.

anatomy.title: Ethmoid · Structure & relationships · draft
anatomy.body: The ethmoid contributes the cribriform plate and perpendicular septal plate. Its superior and middle conchae project into the nasal cavity.
bullets: The inferior nasal concha is a separate bone. Olfactory nerve perforations and individual ethmoid air cells are not certified by this mesh.
Reference bone surface: named landmarks, sutures, internal canals, marrow and cortical thickness are not independently segmented or validated. A cut surface is not an acquired CT section.
Source identity: FMA52740 · 1 source component. Boundaries and attachments require independent review.
anatomy.note: Independent anatomical and clinical review pending. Explode/cut views are not tissue interiors, operative cleavage planes, physiological jaw/swallowing motion or acquired imaging.

function.title: Ethmoid · Role & limits · draft
function.body: Supports the upper nasal framework and the boundary between the nose and anterior cranial region.
bullets: The inferior nasal concha is a separate bone. Olfactory nerve perforations and individual ethmoid air cells are not certified by this mesh.
function.note: Independent anatomical and clinical review pending. Explode/cut views are not tissue interiors, operative cleavage planes, physiological jaw/swallowing motion or acquired imaging.

ct.title: Ethmoid · CT orientation · draft
ct.body: Use coronal images to distinguish the cribriform region, lateral lamella and ethmoid roof, and the thin medial orbital wall. Side-to-side variation matters; the displayed donor is not a surgical map of an individual olfactory fossa.
bullets: The ethmoid contributes the cribriform plate and perpendicular septal plate. Its superior and middle conchae project into the nasal cavity.

On an existing study, correlate bone-window appearances with soft-tissue images and adjacent sections. Atlas colour and cut surfaces are not CT attenuation, cortical thickness or patient-specific findings.
The inferior nasal concha is a separate bone. Olfactory nerve perforations and individual ethmoid air cells are not certified by this mesh.

mri.title: Ethmoid · MRI orientation · draft
mri.body: Review tissue above and below the anterior skull base separately. MRI can clarify intracranial and sinonasal soft-tissue relationships, while the thin bony partitions need CT correlation; a dark boundary alone does not establish a defect or CSF leak.
bullets: The ethmoid contributes the cribriform plate and perpendicular septal plate. Its superior and middle conchae project into the nasal cavity.

Identify the sequence and field of view first. Cortical bone is generally low signal on conventional MRI; marrow and neighbouring soft tissues supply different information. A surface mesh supplies no MR signal.

xray.title: Ethmoid · xray orientation · draft
xray.body: The ethmoid lies between the orbits and contributes to the medial orbital walls. Its air cells are anatomical context. Caldwell and Waters projection descriptions concern orbital and sinus regions, not a proven outline of every ethmoid part.
bullets: The whole-bone mesh does not certify individual air-cell walls or the cribriform plate as separately visible on a radiograph.
An apparent boundary needs its own image context. Selecting this concept does not establish a patient defect, sinus disease or olfactory-pathway finding.
xray.note: Original educational draft; revision-bound radiologist sign-off pending. The cited institutional protocol is a historical projection reference, not current acquisition or diagnostic advice. This static source-labelled mesh is not an X-ray image, patient registration or proof of radiographic visibility. Atlas, case and paid-lecture access remain independent.

pathology.title: Ethmoid · Injury & disease · draft
pathology.body: Cribriform-plate trauma may injure olfactory fibres and can accompany an anterior skull-base injury. A skull-base defect with a cerebrospinal-fluid leak creates a route for infection.
bullets: Clear nasal drainage after head injury requires urgent assessment; appearance alone does not confirm that the fluid is cerebrospinal fluid.
The cribriform region, nasal septal contribution and medial orbital walls belong to one reference bone. No dural defect, olfactory-fibre disruption or sinus infection is reconstructed.
pathology.note: Draft teaching; independent anatomical and clinical review pending. Educational context, not a patient diagnosis or treatment plan.

clinical.title: Ethmoid · Clinical context · draft
clinical.body: Keep the nasal roof and adjacent orbit distinct when considering symptoms after central facial trauma.
bullets: Loss of smell or nasal discharge cannot be localised to this bone from the atlas alone. Patient examination and appropriate testing are needed.
The cribriform region, nasal septal contribution and medial orbital walls belong to one reference bone. No dural defect, olfactory-fibre disruption or sinus infection is reconstructed.
clinical.note: Draft teaching; independent anatomical and clinical review pending. Educational context, not a patient diagnosis or treatment plan.

bullets: Perpendicular plate

quiz.explanation: Small openings in the ethmoid cribriform plate transmit olfactory nerve fibres.

pathology.title: Frontal bone · Injury & disease · draft
pathology.body: Frontal sinus injuries can affect the anterior wall, posterior wall or outflow region differently. A forehead contour defect and a possible communication with the cranial cavity are not equivalent findings.
bullets: Posterior-wall and drainage involvement must be considered separately from the visible external shape.
One frontal-bone mesh is not a validated reconstruction of the sinus walls, drainage route, dura or intracranial contents.
pathology.note: Draft teaching; independent anatomical and clinical review pending. Educational context, not a patient diagnosis or treatment plan.

clinical.title: Frontal bone · Clinical context · draft
clinical.body: Use the frontal bone to orient the forehead, orbital roof and anterior cranial boundary.
bullets: Patient CT can define fracture extent across these areas; selecting or exploding the reference mesh cannot determine sinus drainage or dural integrity.
One frontal-bone mesh is not a validated reconstruction of the sinus walls, drainage route, dura or intracranial contents.
clinical.note: Draft teaching; independent anatomical and clinical review pending. Educational context, not a patient diagnosis or treatment plan.

bullets: The labrum, capsule, bursae and muscle attachment footprints are not validated by the bone outline. Explode distances do not represent scapulohumeral rhythm.

bullets: The spine separates the supraspinous and infraspinous fossae. Follow the blade as well as the lateral processes when checking where a finding lies.

xray.title: Scapula · X-ray orientation

A free-orbit camera is not a prescribed radiographic projection. This surface does not establish a measured joint space or normal alignment.

pathology.body: Scapular fractures after high-energy trauma may accompany chest and other injuries; a scapular selection must not narrow assessment to one bone.
bullets: A glenoid fracture involves the shoulder socket. A scapular-body fracture is not automatically an articular injury.

pathology.title: Left talus · Injury & disease · draft
pathology.body: Talar fractures may disrupt the blood supply and can lead to osteonecrosis. Joint-cartilage damage may also cause post-traumatic arthritis even when a fracture heals.
bullets: These complications are risks, not inevitable outcomes of every talar fracture.
The talar head, neck and body remain one intact source. Ankle and subtalar joints are distinct; no perfusion, collapse or patient fracture is simulated.

ct.title: Left tibia · Proximal tibia · CT comparison · draft

bullets: Orientation task: compare the plateau and underlying proximal bone across the real CT planes, keeping the patient side consistent with the assembled atlas.
Clinical question: CT helps define a proximal tibial fracture. In a plateau injury, ask whether the joint surface is split, depressed or involved in a more complex pattern.
Imaging distinction: multiplanar CT reconstructions contain acquired internal information; the atlas cutaway only hides part of a surface and does not reveal cancellous bone.
Model limit: separation between displayed bones is not a measurement of joint-space loss, plateau depression or instability. No patient-specific fracture or alignment is represented.

pathology.title: Middle phalanx of left third toe · Injury & disease · draft

pathology.title: Middle phalanx of left index finger · Injury & disease · draft
pathology.body: Hyperextension can injure the PIP volar plate, with or without a bony avulsion. Central-slip injury affects the extensor mechanism and may lead to a boutonnière pattern.
bullets: A volar-plate injury and a central-slip injury are not interchangeable explanations for a bent or painful finger.
Middle phalanges exist in digits 2–5, not the thumb. The dorsal central slip and palmar volar plate are different, unvalidated soft-tissue attachments.
pathology.note: Draft teaching; independent anatomical and clinical review pending. Educational context, not a patient diagnosis or treatment plan.

ultrasound.title: Proximal phalanx of left fourth toe · ultrasound evidence & limits · draft
ultrasound.body: A proximal phalanx of a lesser toe runs from its metatarsophalangeal joint to its proximal interphalangeal joint. High-resolution toe ultrasound has described plantar soft-tissue landmarks at the metatarsophalangeal level and along the proximal phalanx in long- and short-axis views. Use the selected toe and joint level to orient any local cortical interval, while keeping the adjacent metatarsal and middle phalanx separate. This whole-bone mesh cannot predict the actual window.
bullets: Name the toe and distinguish the metatarsophalangeal end from the proximal interphalangeal end before comparing views.
Plantar tendon and pulley-region landmarks require acquired images and can be harder to resolve in the fifth toe; they are not mesh parts.
ultrasound.note: Original educational draft; revision-bound radiologist review pending. The selected three-phalangeal lesser-toe pattern is not universal: biphalangeal variants occur, particularly in the fifth toe. The whole-bone mesh is not an ultrasound frame, patient registration, acquisition simulator or diagnostic test. A local acoustic window does not show the entire bone or its marrow. Atlas, imaging-case and paid-lecture access remain independent.

pathology.title: Proximal phalanx of left fourth toe · Injury & disease · draft
pathology.body: Plantar-plate injury can make a lesser MTP joint unstable and allow the toe to drift from its normal position. This is a soft-tissue problem, not necessarily a fractured proximal phalanx.
bullets: Pain or altered toe position alone does not identify the injured tissue.
These proximal phalanges retain their own digits and sides. No plantar-plate tear, MTP dislocation or crossover-toe mechanics are reconstructed.
pathology.note: Draft teaching; independent anatomical and clinical review pending. Educational context, not a patient diagnosis or treatment plan.

clinical.title: Proximal phalanx of left fourth toe · Clinical context · draft
clinical.body: Relate the phalanx base to its metatarsal head, keeping the MTP joint distinct from the PIP joint farther along the toe.
bullets: The model does not perform an instability test or prove that a drifting toe has a plantar-plate tear.
These proximal phalanges retain their own digits and sides. No plantar-plate tear, MTP dislocation or crossover-toe mechanics are reconstructed.
clinical.note: Draft teaching; independent anatomical and clinical review pending. Educational context, not a patient diagnosis or treatment plan.

ultrasound.title: Proximal phalanx of left index finger · ultrasound evidence & limits · draft

anatomy.title: Overview
anatomy.body: A flat triangular bone linking the upper limb to the axial skeleton through the clavicle. Its lateral angle forms the glenoid fossa.
bullets: Borders: superior, medial and lateral
Processes: spine, acromion and coracoid
Articulations: clavicle and humeral head

function.title: Mechanical role
function.body: Provides a mobile platform for glenohumeral motion and a broad attachment surface for stabilising muscles.
bullets: Upward rotation supports arm elevation
Retraction and protraction position the glenoid
Scapulothoracic motion contributes to shoulder rhythm

ct.title: CT appearance
ct.body: Cortical margins are high attenuation with a cancellous medullary centre. Multiplanar review is useful for the glenoid, acromion and fracture planes.
ct.note: Prototype teaching copy — verify against an approved imaging reference and local protocol before clinical release.

mri.title: MRI appearance
mri.body: Marrow signal varies with sequence and age; the cortical shell remains low signal. Review the glenoid labral interface and muscle attachments.

bullets: Compare the glenoid with the humeral head before isolating the scapula. Separation is a study aid and changes their apparent relationship.
A free-orbit camera is not a prescribed radiographic projection. This surface does not establish a measured joint space or normal alignment.

pathology.title: Common patterns
pathology.body: Trauma may involve the body, neck, glenoid or processes. Morphology of the acromion and glenoid can alter shoulder mechanics.
bullets: Scapular fractures
Glenoid rim injury
Os acromiale and degenerative change

clinical.title: Clinical relevance
clinical.body: Scapular position and control are assessed alongside cuff strength and glenohumeral range.
bullets: Look for winging
Compare resting position side-to-side
Correlate focal tenderness with trauma history

xray.title: Right semimembranosus · Ischial tuberosity on X-ray · draft
xray.body: The ischial tuberosity is an indirect bony attachment landmark for the proximal hamstrings, including semimembranosus. A radiograph can show an ossified avulsion in this region; it does not outline the selected individual muscle or establish a tendon tear.
bullets: Orient the right reference structure at the ischial tuberosity. Verify the actual study's side marker and projection; the reference side is not a patient-side match.

Adult cadaveric studies describe a semimembranosus attachment beside the semitendinosus and long-head biceps femoris origins. This supports regional orientation, not a patient-specific footprint or a claim that one fragment identifies semimembranosus alone.

An ischial fragment cannot distinguish which proximal hamstring is involved or establish how many tendons are injured. Retain the distinction between a bony attachment clue and direct soft-tissue assessment.

The radiographic avulsion evidence comes from selected adolescent athletic injury cohorts, not normal muscle-visibility studies or a population survey. Do not extrapolate their frequencies or mechanisms to adults, or infer that a normal film excludes a soft-tissue injury.

bullets: Motor supply: Primarily the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI); cervical-plexus fibres also convey proprioceptive information.
Named nerves are teaching references, not validated nerve courses or motor territories in this muscle entry.

pathology.title: Left sternocleidomastoid · Injury & disease · draft
pathology.body: Cervical dystonia causes involuntary patterned head or neck movement. A torticollis posture is not synonymous with sternocleidomastoid shortening.
bullets: Congenital fibrosis, structural disorders and compensatory postures can mimic dystonia; a static head position is insufficient to distinguish them.
Each side is one source component, not independently segmented sternal/clavicular heads or validated motor territories.

clinical.title: Left sternocleidomastoid · Clinical context · draft

xray.title: Right rectus femoris · Anterior inferior iliac spine on X-ray · draft
xray.body: The anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS) is an indirect bony attachment landmark for the direct head of rectus femoris. A radiograph can show an ossified avulsion fragment in this region; it does not outline the selected individual muscle or establish a tendon tear.
bullets: Orient the right reference structure at the anterior inferior iliac spine. Verify the actual study's side marker and projection; the reference side is not a patient-side match.

Keep the direct-head AIIS attachment distinct from the reflected/indirect origin. An AIIS fragment is not proof that only one head is injured, or that the rest of rectus femoris is intact. The cited MRI injury series assessed the heads separately; a coloured whole-muscle surface does not reproduce that assessment.

Use the AIIS to orient the proximal attachment region, not to label the entire quadriceps on a plain film. Do not transfer a reference-model footprint to a patient radiograph or infer tendon continuity from a normal bony outline.

The radiographic avulsion evidence comes from selected adolescent athletic injury cohorts, not normal muscle-visibility studies or a population survey. Do not extrapolate their frequencies or mechanisms to adults, or infer that a normal film excludes a soft-tissue injury.

Compare the assembled model with an independently verified study only when available. Rotation and explode views do not simulate X-ray attenuation, detector geometry or patient registration. No acquired image, treatment threshold or management protocol is supplied.

function.title: Heart · Circulatory role & visible limits · draft
function.body: Rhythmic contraction of the heart generates pressure for two linked circuits. The right heart receives systemic venous blood and sends it towards the lungs; oxygenated blood returns to the left heart for delivery through the systemic circulation. Coronary vessels supply the heart muscle itself.
bullets: The pulmonary circuit links the right heart with the lungs; the systemic circuit links the left heart with the rest of the body.
The nested cardiac study exposes selected cavities and vessels, but the root and nested surfaces do not animate contraction, valves or blood flow and do not quantify pressure, volume or perfusion.
Source: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute; National Institutes of Health; U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.

pathology.title: Heart · Injury & disease · draft
pathology.body: Myocardial infarction is injury and death of heart muscle after inadequate blood supply. Coronary plaque disruption with clot formation is a common mechanism, but not every infarction involves an obstructive coronary plaque.
bullets: Heart failure concerns inadequate filling or pumping for the body's needs; it does not mean the heart has stopped. A heart attack and cardiac arrest are also different events.
A reference surface cannot establish ischaemia, infarct extent, ejection fraction or an abnormal rhythm.

function.title: Right lung · Respiratory role & visible limits · draft
function.body: Ventilation moves air through the respiratory passages into and out of the lungs. In the alveoli, oxygen moves from inhaled air into blood while carbon dioxide moves from blood into air for exhalation. Air movement depends on the respiratory muscles and open airways; it is distinct from gas transfer across the alveolar surface.

ct.body: The central canal belongs within the spinal cord; it is not the larger vertebral canal enclosing the cord. Do not label the bony canal on CT as this small intramedullary space. A visible atlas surface does not establish that the normal central canal can be resolved on routine CT.
bullets: CT myelography outlines the cord and nerve roots using contrast in the surrounding subarachnoid space. That contrast column is not a cast of the central canal.
MRI is used to assess the cord itself and suspected intramedullary cavities. This anatomical model supplies neither CT attenuation nor a diagnostic exclusion of cord disease.

mri.title: Central canal of spinal cord · MRI: a canal-like signal is not a diagnosis · draft
mri.body: A thin fluid-signal feature within or near the midline of the cord needs anatomical interpretation, not automatic labelling as a syrinx. MRI is the principal imaging method for evaluating syringomyelia, but this source surface is a reference representation, not a segmented cavity from that examination.
bullets: Petit-Lacour and colleagues described appearances compatible with a persistent central canal in 12 of 794 spinal MRI studies. That observational series does not supply a universal size threshold or a patient-specific diagnosis.

An exploratory cervical MRI study found that some canal-like T2 signal may relate to the anterior median fissure. Compare axial and sagittal relationships; a sagittal bright line alone does not establish the precise space.
Do not infer patency, fluid flow, symptoms or treatment from this mesh. Any proposed scan correspondence needs the actual acquisition, annotation and revision-bound radiologist review.

anatomy.title: Cricoid cartilage · Structure & connections · draft
anatomy.body: A complete cartilaginous ring at the lower larynx, with a narrow anterior arch and a broad posterior lamina.
bullets: The selected cricoid groups two source files, FJ2440 and FJ2769. Their union and internal boundaries are not independently validated. This is not a patent airway measurement or procedural landmark certification.
Source identity: FMA9615 · 2 source components. Boundaries and attachments require independent review.
anatomy.note: Independent anatomical and clinical review pending. Explode/cut views are not tissue interiors, normal joint motion, tissue strain or acquired imaging. Recovered source surface. Anatomical boundaries, detail and spatial relationships have not been independently reviewed.

function.title: Cricoid cartilage · Role & limits · draft
function.body: Supports the airway framework and provides articulations and attachment sites for the laryngeal movement apparatus.
bullets: The selected cricoid groups two source files, FJ2440 and FJ2769. Their union and internal boundaries are not independently validated. This is not a patent airway measurement or procedural landmark certification.

ct.title: Cricoid cartilage · CT orientation · draft
ct.body: Look for the cricoid ring below the thyroid cartilage, with a broader posterior lamina and narrower anterior arch. Follow it towards the upper trachea on adjacent sections.
bullets: Two original source components remain grouped as one cricoid identity. They are not certified arch-versus-lamina segments, a complete airway lumen or a measured stenosis.
Reassemble the existing epiglottis/laryngeal study before comparing relationships. Separation distances are display settings, not anatomical measurements.
Ossification varies between individuals and within the laryngeal cartilages. A gap or asymmetric mineralisation alone is not a diagnosis.
ct.note: Original teaching draft for revision-bound radiologist review. No acquired image, validated registration, contouring protocol or airway-management guidance is supplied. Atlas, imaging-case and paid-lecture access remain independent.

mri.title: Cricoid cartilage · MRI orientation · draft
mri.body: Find the cricoid at the lower laryngeal framework on axial T1-weighted images and follow its extent towards the trachea. Its relationship to nearby soft tissues must be checked on the acquired study.
bullets: Two original source components remain grouped as one cricoid identity. They are not certified arch-versus-lamina segments, a complete airway lumen or a measured stenosis.

The cited T1 study compared contours in five patients; it does not validate this mesh, every MRI sequence or automatic scan correspondence.

ultrasound.title: Cricoid cartilage · Ultrasound orientation · draft
ultrasound.body: The transverse cricoid appearance includes a hypoechoic anterior arch. A posterior air–mucosa interface and reverberation boundary should not be mistaken for an image of the entire posterior cartilage ring.
bullets: This is a static reference surface, not vocal-fold motion, nerve function, a diagnosis, a registered scan or a probe-plane model. No procedural guidance is supplied.
The anatomical ultrasound study examined 100 healthy volunteers and excluded short neck, morbid obesity and abnormal airway anatomy; its observations do not establish visibility in every patient.
Air limits deeper visibility. Calcification may limit the thyroid window; an unseen structure is not evidence of absence.

pathology.title: Cricoid cartilage · Injury & disease · draft
pathology.body: Laryngeal trauma can involve cartilage, joints, mucosa, ligaments or nerves, with different consequences for breathing, swallowing and voice. A normal-looking exterior framework does not rule out an important internal injury.
bullets: Voice change and noisy or difficult breathing after neck trauma require attention even without an obvious external deformity.
The thyroid, cricoid, arytenoid, corniculate and cuneiform selections do not share one identical injury pattern.
Eight cartilage identities, nine source components. Mucosal coverage, joint surfaces and dynamic airway behaviour are not fully validated; no patient-specific trauma or procedural simulation.
pathology.note: Draft teaching; independent anatomical and clinical review pending. Educational context, not a patient diagnosis or treatment plan. Recovered source surface. Anatomical boundaries, detail and spatial relationships have not been independently reviewed.

clinical.title: Cricoid cartilage · Clinical context · draft
clinical.body: Breathing difficulty after neck trauma is an emergency. Assessment prioritises the airway and uses specialist examination and imaging as appropriate; do not press on or manipulate the model's corresponding landmarks to test a real injury.
bullets: The cricoid remains one selection with two indexed components, not two separate cartilages.

anatomy.body: A paired cartilage on the upper cricoid lamina. Its vocal process attaches to the vocal ligament; its muscular process receives cricoarytenoid muscle attachments.

ct.title: Right arytenoid cartilage · CT orientation · draft
ct.body: Orient the arytenoid in relation to the cricoid across adjacent CT sections. The cricoarytenoid saddle joint can superimpose on axial images, obscuring its interspace; an absent gap on one section does not establish ankylosis.

anatomy.title: Right long plantar ligament · Anatomy & relationships · draft
anatomy.body: The long plantar ligament spans the sole from the calcaneus to the cuboid, with superficial fibres continuing toward the lateral metatarsal bases.
bullets: Its superficial extension contributes to a tunnel for the fibularis longus tendon. The short plantar ligament lies deeper; neither should be confused with the plantar aponeurosis.
This selection does not separately show deep/superficial fascicles or validate each attachment footprint. A nearby tendon surface does not prove a complete tunnel.
Source identity: FMA44249 · 1 source component. A surface count is not a count of tissue layers or validated attachments.
anatomy.note: Independent anatomical and clinical review pending. Explode/clipping controls are teaching aids, not physiological deformation, acquired imaging or procedure guidance. Recovered source surface. Anatomical boundaries, detail and spatial relationships have not been independently reviewed.

function.title: Long plantar ligament · draft
function.body: The long plantar ligament supports the plantar aspect of the lateral foot and contributes to longitudinal-arch stability.
function.note: Source surface and draft teaching note require independent anatomical review.

ct.title: Right long plantar ligament · CT plantar midfoot orientation · draft
ct.body: On an already acquired foot CT that includes the plantar midfoot, first identify the calcaneus, cuboid and calcaneocuboid joint on serial sections and reformats. These bony landmarks orient the long plantar ligament region; the atlas surface is not a segmented patient ligament.
bullets: The long and short plantar ligaments are distinct, variably shaped supports around the calcaneocuboid joint. Do not infer a tear from the atlas outline or an indistinct CT soft-tissue margin.

CT clarifies adjacent bone and joint relationships. In chronic foot pain with suspected soft-tissue origin after negative or indeterminate radiographs, ACR favours MRI and ultrasound over CT. CT alone does not establish ligament integrity.
ct.note: Original educational draft for revision-bound radiologist review. No CT scan is loaded or registered to this source mesh; this is not an acquisition recommendation or clinical approval. Atlas, imaging-case and paid-lecture access remain independent.

mri.title: Right long plantar ligament · MRI connective-tissue orientation · draft
mri.body: MRI-anatomy correlation of the transverse-tarsal ligament complex helps distinguish the plantar calcaneocuboid region from neighbouring stabilisers. The long plantar selection is an anatomical orientation aid within that region, not the entire complex.
bullets: The long plantar ligament links plantar calcaneus and cuboid with the lateral metatarsal bases. Keep it distinct from the short plantar and spring ligaments when comparing the transverse-tarsal region.

The cited study used ten fresh cadaveric feet, high-resolution MRI before and after joint contrast, and matched anatomical analysis. Its detailed visibility cannot be assumed for every routine clinical acquisition.

Keep the source ligament separate from the short plantar ligament and spring complex; do not transfer a finding or an attachment measurement from one to another. A displayed continuous surface does not grade a tear or prove joint stability.
Source limit: This is one supplied ligament surface, not individually segmented fascicles, a complete plantar ligament complex or a patient-specific attachment map.
mri.note: Introductory teaching for revision-bound radiologist review. Compare anatomy with separation at zero; cutaway is not a scan. No patient images, registration, diagnostic protocol or clinical approval. Case, Atlas and paid-lecture access remain independent.

xray.title: Right long plantar ligament · X-ray bony orientation · draft
xray.body: Locate the calcaneus–cuboid joint in the lateral column of the foot, then the cuboid and metatarsal bases. These bones orient the plantar neighborhood of the long plantar ligament. Transferring a dissection relationship to a radiograph is an anatomical inference, not direct depiction of the ligament or its attachment margins.
bullets: In an 18-cadaver-foot experiment with a radiopaque-painted cuboid surface, an oblique projection reduced overlap at the calcaneocuboid joint. This studied bony joint-line visualization, not long-plantar-ligament visibility or diagnostic performance in patients.

A separate 50-leg dissection series found different long-plantar shapes and fibers blending with the fibularis (peroneus) longus canal before reaching metatarsal bases. Do not impose one fixed distal footprint on a plain film.

Long and short plantar ligaments are distinct components of the plantar calcaneocuboid complex; the shorter component lies deep to the long plantar ligament. Naming their shared bony neighborhood does not separate their fibers on X-ray.
This is a bony orientation exercise. Joint alignment alone cannot establish this particular ligament’s continuity, tear status or the accuracy of its recovered 3D boundary.
xray.note: Original source-bound educational draft; revision-bound radiologist review pending. Bony orientation is not validated ligament visibility. Existing recovered CC-BY-4.0 source boundaries remain unvalidated. No scan, figure, patient example, acquisition instruction, diagnosis or spatial registration is imported or implied. Atlas, imaging-case and paid-lecture access remain independent.

ultrasound.title: Right long plantar ligament · ultrasound evidence & limits · draft
ultrasound.body: For plantar-hindfoot orientation, relate the long plantar ligament to the cuboid and peroneus longus tendon. The ligament crosses superficial to that tendon toward the metatarsal bases; the short plantar ligament is deeper at the calcaneocuboid joint. An illustrated ultrasound review describes this approach but notes that separating the two ligaments can be difficult.
bullets: Do not confuse the long plantar ligament with the plantar fascia or the short plantar ligament.
This source is one gross surface: fibre layers, anisotropy, tenderness and dynamic ligament integrity are not encoded.
A review illustration is not a diagnostic-accuracy study. The separate CT lesson remains pending rather than borrowing ultrasound evidence.
ultrasound.note: Original educational draft; revision-bound radiologist review pending. This unregistered surface model is not an ultrasound frame, acquisition simulator or diagnostic test. Atlas, case and paid-lecture access remain independent.

pathology.title: Right long plantar ligament · Injury & disease · draft
pathology.body: The long plantar ligament belongs to the plantar calcaneocuboid support complex. Injury assessment must distinguish it from the short plantar ligament, spring ligament and plantar fascia; these are not interchangeable labels for plantar foot pain.
bullets: Cadaveric research documents variation in the ligament's shape. Shape variation alone is not proof of a tear or a painful disorder.
The reference surface does not establish whether this ligament is injured or explain an individual patient's arch shape.
One indexed ligament surface per side. Fibre bundles, attachment footprints and adjacent tissue continuity are not independently validated; no load-bearing simulation or procedural guidance.
pathology.note: Draft teaching; independent anatomical and clinical review pending. Educational context, not a patient diagnosis or treatment plan. Recovered source surface. Anatomical boundaries, detail and spatial relationships have not been independently reviewed.

clinical.title: Right long plantar ligament · Clinical context · draft
clinical.body: Use the assembled plantar view to locate the long plantar ligament relative to the calcaneus and cuboid. Clinical localisation requires assessment of neighbouring joints, tendons and other ligaments, not simply selecting the nearest visible surface.
bullets: Explode separates structures for viewing; it does not reproduce ligament stretch or test arch stability.
This selection is not a diagnosis of plantar fasciitis, and no isolated-ligament injury grade is assigned.
One indexed ligament surface per side. Fibre bundles, attachment footprints and adjacent tissue continuity are not independently validated; no load-bearing simulation or procedural guidance.
clinical.note: Draft teaching; independent anatomical and clinical review pending. Educational context, not a patient diagnosis or treatment plan. Recovered source surface. Anatomical boundaries, detail and spatial relationships have not been independently reviewed.

anatomy.title: Prostate · Position and duct relationship · draft
anatomy.body: The prostate lies below the bladder, in front of the rectum, and surrounds the first part of the male urethra. Its base faces upward toward the bladder and its apex downward. Small gland ducts open into the prostatic urethra.
bullets: Conceptual zones: peripheral posterior and lateral tissue; central tissue around the ejaculatory ducts; transition tissue around the proximal urethra; and supporting anterior fibromuscular stroma. These zones are not separately segmented.
This gland is distinct from the seminal vesicles behind the bladder.

anatomy.title: Left testis · Scrotal gonad and internal pathway · draft
anatomy.body: Each testis lies in the scrotum, outside the pelvic cavity. Its tunica albuginea sends partitions inward, forming lobules with seminiferous tubules. The usual outlet sequence proceeds through straight tubules, rete testis and efferent ducts toward the epididymis.
bullets: Pelvis is the navigation group, not a claim that the testis is intrapelvic.

function.title: Left testis · Sperm and androgen production · draft

function.title: Right seminal vesicle · Contribution to semen · draft
function.body: The seminal vesicles add fructose-containing fluid to semen, providing an energy source for sperm. They supply secretions rather than producing sperm. pathology.title: Left common carotid artery · Injury & disease · draft
pathology.body: Carotid atherosclerosis can narrow the arterial pathway or contribute embolic material to downstream brain arteries. These are different mechanisms of reduced cerebral blood supply. A common carotid selection is not a map of a patient's plaque or the cause of every stroke.
bullets: The common trunk and internal/external carotid divisions must not be treated as interchangeable labels.
Thrombosis at one site and embolism from elsewhere require different clinical explanations.

bullets: Cadaveric studies document variation in the profunda origin and in whether the lateral circumflex femoral artery arises from profunda or directly from femoral artery. The usual branching pattern is a guide, not proof of this source anatomy.

The retained deep femoral selection includes a lateral circumflex parent that is not separately selectable. Selection alone cannot resolve that parent’s origin or verify any small branch junction on angiography.

xray.title: Right great saphenous vein · Great saphenous vein · contrast X-ray orientation · draft
xray.body: The great saphenous vein follows a superficial medial lower-limb route toward the femoral venous system. anatomy.title: Right calcaneal tendon · Anatomy & relationships · draft
anatomy.body: The calcaneal (Achilles) tendon continues from gastrocnemius and soleus down the back of the distal leg to attach to the posterior calcaneus.
bullets: It connects calf muscle force to the heel across the back of the ankle. It is tendon tissue, not a ligament joining two bones.
Subtendons, paratenon, bursae and a validated insertion footprint are not independently resolved. Exploding this surface does not model tendon strain or rupture.

ct.title: Right calcaneal tendon · CT: tendon contour versus spectral reconstruction · draft
ct.body: Follow the posterior tendon towards the calcaneus in the assembled model. CT can place tendon contours beside bone, but a colour-coded dual-energy reconstruction is not a direct view of tendon fibres or the same thing as this surface model.
bullets: A prospective single-centre feasibility study compared dual-energy CT with MRI in 22 patients. Its non-specific fat-map application assessed tendon abnormalities; false-positive appearances occurred. Do not generalise this result to conventional CT or treat a map as proof of a tear.

The author’s subsequent reply reaffirmed the importance of clinical examination, ultrasound and MRI. This experimental CT application is not a recommendation to replace those assessments. CT involves ionising radiation; an attractive reconstruction alone does not justify an examination.

Model limit: no patient attenuation, spectral data, tear gap or internal fibres are supplied. Explode distance is a display setting, not tendon retraction. Review actual images and acquisition details independently.

mri.title: Right calcaneal tendon · MRI comparison guide · draft
mri.body: Start with the assembled tendon behind the ankle and follow it towards the heel. Use this 3D relationship to orient yourself before reviewing a real MRI; rotating the model does not select an MRI slice.
bullets: Planes: sagittal images follow the tendon along its length; axial images show its cross-section. The referenced university protocol also includes coronal imaging. Check the actual series orientation and side markers rather than assuming that screen-left is patient-left.

Sequences: the referenced protocol combines T1, proton-density and fat-suppressed T2 imaging. These are different acquisitions, not colour presets for this surface. The local imaging team determines the examination protocol.
Clinical question: MRI can help establish the location and extent of a tear and assess alternative injuries. The atlas cannot measure a patient’s tear, retraction or tendon quality.
Model limits: subtendons, paratenon and the tendon–bone insertion microstructure are not separately segmented. A surface cutaway has no MR signal or internal tissue information.
mri.note: Original teaching draft; independent anatomical, radiological and educator review pending. No patient images, measurements or registered correspondence are loaded. This is not a diagnostic report or a scanning competency assessment.

xray.title: Right calcaneal tendon · X-ray orientation · draft
xray.body: Use the posterior calcaneus to orient the heel attachment of the selected calcaneal (Achilles) tendon. A lateral ankle radiograph may show the tendon-region soft-tissue outline and the adjacent pre-Achilles fat-pad lucency, often called Kager's triangle. These are projectional clues, not the individual subtendons or the coloured atlas surface.
bullets: Altered Kager fat-pad appearance can accompany an acute rupture, but a retrospective case-control study found both missed ruptures and positive signs in ankle-sprain controls. Neither a preserved triangle nor its obscuration alone settles tendon integrity.

An insertional avulsion may include a visible bone fragment at the heel attachment. Absence of that fragment does not exclude a tendon tear elsewhere; plain films do not grade a partial tear or measure a tendon gap.
Ultrasound or MRI can assess tendon soft tissues when clinically indicated. This lesson does not select a scan protocol, diagnose a rupture or replace clinical assessment.

ultrasound.title: Right calcaneal tendon · Ultrasound comparison guide · draft
ultrasound.body: Use the posterior 3D view to locate the Achilles tendon between the calf and heel. In ultrasound, a long-axis view follows the tendon; a short-axis view crosses it. Neither is produced by the atlas camera.
bullets: Coverage: the ESSR guide follows the tendon from the muscle–tendon junction to its calcaneal insertion in both planes, with attention to its surrounding tissues and bursae. This model does not separately show those envelopes or bursae.

Pitfall: beam angle can create a dark area through anisotropy rather than injury. A trained examiner assesses the appearance across views and probe angles; the atlas does not simulate an ultrasound beam.

Pitfall: an intact plantaris tendon can be mistaken for remaining Achilles fibres after a complete tear. Identifying a nearby cord or an intact-looking atlas surface does not demonstrate Achilles continuity.
Dynamic assessment: real-time ultrasound can assess tendon behaviour with ankle movement. Explode is only a viewing arrangement, not a dynamic test, tear gap or measure of mechanical function.

pathology.title: Right calcaneal tendon · Injury & disease · draft
pathology.body: Achilles tendinopathy and an Achilles rupture are different clinical problems. Persistent tendon pain may occur at or above the heel attachment; a rupture is a partial or complete loss of tendon continuity and may cause sudden loss of effective push-off.
bullets: A rupture may follow a sudden pop and swelling, but symptoms alone do not determine tear extent.
The calcaneal tendon selection is the Achilles tendon, not the plantar fascia or a calf-muscle belly.
One indexed tendon surface per side. Subtendons, paratenon and enthesis are not separately segmented; no ultrasound/MRI study or patient registration has been added.

clinical.title: Right calcaneal tendon · Clinical context · draft
clinical.body: A sudden injury with a pop and difficulty pushing off or standing on tiptoe warrants prompt medical assessment. Examination, sometimes supported by ultrasound or MRI, distinguishes tendon disruption from other causes of posterior ankle pain.
bullets: A rendered continuous surface cannot rule out a real tear, and remaining ankle movement does not measure tendon integrity here.

anatomy.title: Right trochlear nerve · Course & identity · draft
anatomy.body: CN IV emerges from the dorsal midbrain, curves around it and follows the cavernous-sinus lateral wall toward the superior orbital fissure.
bullets: The nuclear fibres cross before emergence. The side of this selected peripheral source segment does not independently identify its nucleus or validate the complete intracranial route.

function.title: Trochlear nerve (CN IV) · draft
function.body: The trochlear nerve supplies the superior oblique muscle of the eye. It emerges from the dorsal brainstem and reaches the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.
function.note: The displayed source segment is not a validated reconstruction of the entire nerve course.

ct.title: Right trochlear nerve · CT orientation · draft
ct.body: CN IV courses through the lateral sector of the superior orbital fissure outside the annulus before crossing toward the superior oblique muscle. The fissure is the CT landmark; the illustrated nerve course comes from anatomy and should not be read as a line identified on CT.
bullets: Source-bound static anatomy only. Restore assembled separation before comparing relationships; explode and isolate are model controls, not CT planes. No scan, patient registration, pathology assessment or nerve-function inference is supplied.
The dissection places the optic strut between the optic canal and superior orbital fissure. Relating that anatomy to the CT landmarks is an educational comparison, not a branch-level CT annotation.

Daniels et al. correlated coronal CT with cadaver sections and illustrated apical anatomy in clinical CT. This does not establish routine visibility of any named small branch, diagnostic sensitivity, or an acquisition protocol.
ct.note: Original educational source draft; revision-bound radiologist review and sign-off are pending. Atlas, imaging-case and paid-lecture access remain independent.

mri.title: Right trochlear nerve · MRI orientation · draft

pathology.title: Right trochlear nerve · Injury & disease · draft
pathology.body: Trochlear palsy can produce vertical or oblique binocular diplopia, often troublesome when reading or looking down.
bullets: Congenital/decompensated and acquired causes differ. Superior-oblique weakness can also be mimicked by muscle or neuromuscular disease.
CN IV is distinct from the supratrochlear and infratrochlear sensory nerves. The selected side is a peripheral source label, not a mapped nuclear lesion.

clinical.title: Right trochlear nerve · Clinical context · draft
clinical.body: Relate impaired depression of the adducted eye to superior-oblique function; not every vertical misalignment is a fourth-nerve palsy.

pathology.title: Left epididymis · Injury & disease · draft
pathology.body: Epididymitis is inflammation of the epididymis, often due to infection. Sexually transmitted and urinary infections are possible causes; the label alone does not establish the organism.
bullets: Pain and swelling can overlap with other scrotal disorders.
Clinical history and testing are needed to establish the cause.

anatomy.body: The male urethra leads from the bladder to the external opening. Its usual regions are prostatic, membranous through the pelvic floor, and spongy through the penis. The ureters instead bring urine to the bladder.

pathology.title: Urethra · Injury & disease · draft
pathology.body: Urethral stricture narrows the urine outflow passage, often through scarring after injury or inflammation. Urinary retention may result from an outlet blockage, but inadequate bladder contraction is another mechanism.
bullets: A urethral narrowing is distinct from an obstructed ureter between kidney and bladder.
This surface does not show a stricture, establish its length or measure urinary flow.

quiz.title: Urethra · Pelvic duct quick check · draft
quiz.body: Which statement distinguishes the adult male urethra from a ureter?
bullets: Both carry urine directly from kidney to bladder
The urethra produces sperm
The urethra carries urine outward from the bladder and also conveys semen
The ureter normally carries semen through the prostate
quiz.correctAnswer: The urethra carries urine outward from the bladder and also conveys semen
quiz.explanation: A ureter connects a kidney with the bladder. The male urethra is the outlet for urine and also a reproductive passage for semen. This shared role does not mean simultaneous flow, and the surface model does not demonstrate patency.

bullets: The normal disc series begins below the axis, at C2–C3; there is no intervertebral disc between atlas and axis. Disc joints are distinct from the posterior synovial facet joints.

bullets: Intervertebral discs are fibrocartilaginous joints between vertebral bodies. An outer annulus surrounds an inner nucleus; together they help cushion and distribute load while allowing movement between bodies.
Compare the selected disc with the neighbouring bodies as a functional unit, without assigning a patient imaging interval from its source name.

bullets: Intervertebral discs are fibrocartilaginous joints between vertebral bodies. An outer annulus surrounds an inner nucleus; together they help cushion and distribute load while allowing movement between bodies.

The tested pressure pattern depended on direction and region; one fixed value would obscure those differences.
The experiment retained short rib stumps rather than an intact rib cage, so it does not supply universal motion or force claims for patients.

function.title: Intervertebral disk of sixth thoracic vertebra · Function · draft

xray.title: Right thyrocervical trunk · contrast arterial X-ray orientation · draft
xray.body: The thyrocervical trunk usually arises from the first subclavian segment and gives branches toward the lower neck and scapular region; its branch pattern can vary.
bullets: Unenhanced plain radiography does not outline a normal branch lumen. Contrast arteriography, including DSA, differs from CTA/MRA and injected cadaver radiography.

The right atlas label is not an acquired side marker; check examination side and projection independently.

ultrasound.title: Right thyrocervical trunk · ultrasound orientation · draft
ultrasound.body: The thyrocervical trunk is a short branch in the lower-neck subclavian region. A published sonographic observation in one adult placed it relative to the subclavian artery and internal jugular vein, and distinguished it from the nearby vertebral artery. This is an orientation example from one examination, not a standardized detection rate or a fixed depth for either side. The atlas surface supplies a named branch to compare conceptually with an acquired scan, but cannot determine the actual branch origin in that scan.
bullets: If visible, use continuity with the acquired subclavian image to distinguish the trunk from a nearby vertebral or other arterial signal.
Branching and acoustic access may differ. Do not transfer the reported volunteer position or depth into a learner case as a patient-specific measurement.
The displayed surface does not validate its complete daughter branches, Doppler flow, patency or a safe intervention path.
ultrasound.note: Original educational draft; revision-bound radiologist sign-off pending. This source-labelled reference surface supplies no sonogram, Doppler pixels or measurement and has no patient-to-atlas registration. pathology.title: Right thyrocervical trunk · Injury & disease · draft
pathology.body: Thyrocervical trunk injury can produce a pseudoaneurysm and bleeding at the root of the neck. Case reports describe delayed presentations and blood entering the pleural space; a small external wound does not define the depth of injury.
bullets: Pseudoaneurysm is a contained arterial leak, not a normal branch junction.
Rare reports do not establish a screening schedule or universal mechanism.
Separate thyrocervical trunks with shoulder-arm/head-neck/thorax navigation; no complete neck branches, airway compression model or puncture corridor.
pathology.note: Draft teaching; independent anatomical and clinical review pending. Educational context, not a patient diagnosis or treatment plan. Independently selectable source segment, not a complete branching tree. Gaps are not reconstructed and vessel calibre is not certified. Source version 4.0 surface in its unchanged common frame. clinical.title: Right thyrocervical trunk · Clinical context · draft

ultrasound.title: Right costocervical trunk · ultrasound orientation · draft
ultrasound.body: A sonographic mapping study of the brachial plexus used the deep cervical artery as a landmark near the lower cervical roots and described it as arising from the costocervical artery. That observation concerns a daughter branch, not documented detection of the complete costocervical parent. The source-labelled parent trunk can orient an anatomy discussion about the subclavian and deep cervical pathways, but a branch signal must not be promoted into proof of the whole trunk or its exact junction in an individual scan.
bullets: Keep the deep cervical landmark and the costocervical parent distinct when reading an acquired image; follow the visible continuity before assigning a vessel name.
A reported relationship near C7 and C8 is an anatomical orientation, not proof that these roots or their neighbouring artery are resolved in every examination.
The static model gives no sonographic detection rate, patient-specific depth, full parent course, Doppler result or validated nerve geometry.

bullets: Blood in the pleural space is different from a normal vessel lying near the pleura.
A single case cannot establish rupture frequency or screening policy.

pathology.title: Right medial geniculate body · Injury & disease · draft
pathology.body: Published human cases describe hearing difficulty after bilateral medial-geniculate infarction and altered sound perception after a unilateral lesion.

ct.title: Flexor retinaculum of right wrist · CT carpal-tunnel orientation · draft
ct.body: On an already acquired wrist CT, use axial sections to follow the palmar carpal arch around the tunnel and the position of the retinacular roof. This is an orientation to the osseous corridor, not a measurement of median-nerve compression.

bullets: Bowing alone is not a diagnosis of carpal tunnel syndrome. This historical normal-anatomy study does not supply a universal measurement threshold for current clinical examinations.

xray.title: Flexor retinaculum of right wrist · X-ray bony orientation · draft
xray.body: Use the carpal bones to orient the volar wrist: scaphoid and trapezium on the radial side, pisiform and hamate on the ulnar side. Anatomical research places a deeper transverse fibrous lamina between these bones. Relating that anatomy to projected bony landmarks is an educational inference, not a validated X-ray outline of the retinaculum.
bullets: Bone profiles depend on projection and overlap. A projected bone edge does not specify a ligament insertion footprint or the full source-mesh boundary.

A dissection/histology study with MRI correlation distinguished superficial fascial reinforcement from the deeper transverse carpal ligament. The broad source label “flexor retinaculum” does not prove that this mesh is only that deeper lamina.

One published left-wrist case had no hook-of-hamate abnormality on a dedicated radiograph, yet a partial retinacular attachment tear was described on MRI. This exceptional case illustrates why a normal-looking bony landmark cannot certify soft-tissue integrity; it supplies no prevalence or sensitivity estimate.
xray.note: Original source-bound educational draft; revision-bound radiologist review pending. Bony orientation is not validated ligament visibility. pathology.title: Flexor retinaculum of right wrist · Injury & disease · draft
pathology.body: Carpal tunnel syndrome concerns compression of the median nerve at the wrist beneath the transverse carpal ligament, within the flexor-retinaculum region. The selected retinacular surface is a boundary landmark, not a diseased nerve or a measure of tunnel pressure.
bullets: Symptoms may include tingling or numbness in the thumb, index and middle fingers and the thumb-side of the ring finger.
Not all hand numbness is carpal tunnel syndrome; a broad symptom distribution needs clinical assessment.
One indexed retinacular surface per side. Regional thickness, attachments and individual fascial subdivisions are not clinically validated; no tunnel-pressure or nerve-conduction simulation.

ct.title: Right iliotibial tract · CT lateral knee orientation · draft

mri.title: Right iliotibial tract · MRI connective-tissue orientation · draft
mri.body: Separate proximal iliac-crest assessment from distal lateral-knee assessment. Pelvic MRI and cadaveric work localised proximal tract attachment around the iliac tubercle; a knee examination does not represent that proximal region.
bullets: The iliotibial tract is part of the fascia lata, with fibrous anchorage to the distal femur. Its relationship to the lateral femoral epicondyle is not that of a free cord sliding over bone.

Distal MRI research depicts deep femoral attachment bands and the capsulo-osseous layer, including low-signal bands in non-pivot-shift examples. These finer structures are not separately delineated by this broad tract mesh.

The distal study compared twenty knees without a pivot-shift marrow-oedema pattern with twenty showing that pattern. These selected cohorts do not establish an injury in this donor or a population-wide normal reference.

xray.title: Right iliotibial tract · X-ray orientation · draft

Use the proximal tibial bone as an X-ray orientation landmark; a plain film does not display the complete fascial band, its separate layers or an attachment footprint matching this mesh.
bullets: A reported Gerdy-tubercle avulsion was visible on radiographs and confirmed with CT; MRI assessed associated soft tissues. That unusual isolated case illustrates a bony clue, not a rule that such injuries are isolated or that a normal radiograph excludes an iliotibial-tract injury.

Do not equate every lateral tibial fragment with the same injury. Gerdy-tubercle and Segond avulsions require attention to the actual donor site and associated findings. Cadaveric/MR research found iliotibial fibres extending behind Gerdy's tubercle and attaching to some Segond fragments, so an absolute “Segond never involves the iliotibial tract” rule is incorrect.

ct.title: Right common tendinous ring · CT orientation · draft
ct.body: The common tendinous-ring region is at the orbital apex, around the orbital opening of the optic canal and the central superior orbital fissure. The optic strut separates the canal from the fissure. Compare these landmarks with the assembled model for orientation. This is anatomical location teaching, not direct tendon depiction on CT; the selected tendon surface is not a contour identified on CT.
bullets: Source-bound static anatomy only. Restore assembled separation before comparing relationships; explode and isolate are model controls, not CT planes. No acquired-image annotation or patient registration is supplied.

Evidence of depiction is not a routine-visibility promise. Daniels et al. correlated coronal cadaver CT with sections and demonstrated apical annulus anatomy in selected clinical CT studies. The inspected abstract does not establish whether individual ring fibres or their precise boundaries are separable on a particular scan, nor a diagnostic sensitivity or protocol.

The detailed annular boundary is disputed. Naito et al. found a shared C-shaped origin for three recti with an independent superior rectus origin; Lacey et al. found a common tendinous origin. Ma et al. described posterior fibrous origins joining into a complete ring further anteriorly. These anatomical studies do not validate the topology, thickness or attachment footprint of this source mesh.

Keep the tendon region distinct from the optic nerve, rectus muscles and bony openings. Their proximity may help explain location but cannot substitute for direct tendon identification. Evidence of depiction is not a routine-visibility promise. Daniels et al. correlated coronal cadaver CT with sections and demonstrated apical annulus anatomy in selected clinical CT studies. The detailed annular boundary is disputed. Naito et al. found a shared C-shaped origin for three recti with an independent superior rectus origin; Lacey et al. found a common tendinous origin. mri.title: Right plantar arch · MRI / MRA orientation · draft
mri.body: A routine foot MRI and a dedicated pedal MRA answer different questions. For spatial learning, identify the side and dorsal/plantar orientation, then trace the candidate artery through acquired source sections before comparing it with this donor surface. A single projection or neighbouring signal focus is not enough to name a small branch.
bullets: The plantar arterial arch joins lateral plantar and deep plantar contributions. Cadaveric work describes variable contributions; a donor-labelled arch does not define the branching pattern of every foot.
Independent original right source FMA43943: FJ2169. The opposite side is another donor-source selection, not a mirrored substitute or patient contour.

An older comparative time-of-flight study examined medial plantar, lateral plantar and arch vessels in patients with arterial occlusive disease. Its findings concern that acquisition and cohort, not routine foot MRI or guaranteed visibility of every branch.

A distal-extremity MRA study reported difficulty depicting flow in the plantar arch and retrograde lateral plantar flow. Apparent signal loss therefore needs acquisition-specific assessment; it is not automatically an occluded or absent artery.

Trace the parent and arch on the actual acquisition. Motion, sequence sensitivity and overlapping venous signal can limit interpretation; missing atlas tributaries and endpoint gaps are not scan findings.
Return separation to zero before comparing anatomical relationships. Explode, clipping and camera movement do not supply an MRI slice plane or a patient-to-atlas transform.
mri.note: Original educational draft; revision-bound radiologist sign-off pending, with no clinical or imaging approval. No acquisition protocol, diagnostic cutoff, perfusion assessment, complete digital supply or revascularisation target is inferred. Atlas, case and paid-lecture access remain independent.

xray.title: Right plantar arch · X-ray arterial orientation · draft
xray.body: Cadaveric work describes variable deep plantar and lateral plantar contributions to the arch. Use this source-labelled surface for orientation, not as a universal complete pedal circulation or proof that an acquired angiogram shows the same configuration.
bullets: Plain foot radiographs can show arterial-wall calcification; this is not a contrast-filled lumen examination or validation that this individual source-labelled branch is visible.

For a future cleared contrast-angiography comparison, confirm the patient, side, projection and opacified channel. A static mesh cannot establish patency, arch completeness, collateral flow or a treatment target.
xray.note: Independent anatomy/radiology review pending. Reading references only: no acquired images, contrast lumen, diagnosis, procedural planning, paid-lecture access or validated scan registration. Ordinary radiography and contrast angiography are distinct examinations.

ultrasound.title: Right plantar arch · Ultrasound arterial orientation · draft
ultrasound.body: The plantar arch can be oriented from the lateral plantar artery toward the first intermetatarsal space. In a plantar ultrasound view it lies deeper relative to the plantar fascia than the lateral plantar artery. This arch selection is not the separate deep plantar connecting artery.
bullets: The reference is an illustrated anatomy/technique review, not a prospective diagnostic-accuracy study or validation of these meshes.

The static source does not contain Doppler flow, waveforms, patency, perfusion or a validated lumen. Restore assembled positions before comparing relationships; apparent display gaps are not evidence of occlusion.
A named source vessel does not establish its visibility or continuity on a patient study. There is no acquired ultrasound image or validated probe plane connected here.
